newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil firms sell-off to aid infrastructure - Kandir.
newsitem.headline: Brazil firms sell-off to aid infrastructure - Kandir.

text.p: Receipts from Brazil's privatization program will continue to be used to reduce the country's debt stockpile but some will also be pumped into infrastructure projects, Planning Minister Antonio Kandir said.

In an interview with newspaper Gazeta Mercantil, Kandir said the $10 billion expected from federal privatizations in 1997 would be used to reduce debt, boost infrastructure and attract some of the foreign capital needed to finance Brazil's current account deficit.

"There are therefore three possible paths for the National Privatization Program," Kandir told Gazeta. "Sell and send the assets to the National Treasury, buy government debt in the market or create a fund to finance private sector investments."

Leading figures within the government have recently been at odds over what to do with privatization receipts. Finance Minister Pedro Malan, a stickler for monetary prudence, argues that all the receipts be used to reduce Brazil's debt stockpile.

But other cabinet members, like Communications Minister Sergio Motta, prefer the idea of using the revenues to bolster Brazil's ailing infrastructure. Powerful senators have also demanded that some receipts from the upcoming privatization of mining Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) giant be channeled into projects in their regions.

Kandir told Gazeta the government was still mulling over details but the idea was to create two funds offering credit to the private sector infrastructure projects. The funds would probably be set up in time for the privatization of CVRD, expected to begin in March and which may raise about $5.0 billion, he told Gazeta.
Interest charged would be linked to the rate the government pays on its debt and would "certainly" be higher than the dividends CVRD pays to the federal government, Kandir said.
Government officials say CVRD pays yearly revenues of about $80 million, or two percent of assets, to Brasilia.

Brazil expects federal privatization receipts to top $10 billion in 1997, up from $4.5 billion in 1996. As well as CVRD, the privatization program will encompass ports, power companies, sewage and telecommunications firms, Kandir said.
